props.title: What's Love Got to Do with It
props.initialSlug: Tina Turner's rise from abuse to music legend

sections.content: What's Love Got to Do with It (1993) delivers one of the most powerful performances in biographical film history, with Angela Bassett's explosive portrayal of Tina Turner's transformation from Anna Mae Bullock to global superstar. The film brutally chronicles the abuse she suffered at the hands of Ike Turner (Laurence Fishburne) while revolutionizing the musical biopic genre through its unflinching examination of domestic violence. Like Lady Sings the Blues (1972) before it, the film refuses to sanitize its subject's struggles, but distinguishes itself by focusing on survival rather than tragedy.

sections.content: The film's impact rippled through Hollywood, paving the way for grittier musical biopics that didn't shy away from darkness. Ray (2004) and Walk the Line (2005) followed its template of exploring both artistic genius and personal demons. But what sets What's Love Got to Do with It apart is its laser focus on domestic violence and female empowerment, themes that wouldn't become mainstream in Hollywood for decades. Bassett's physical transformation and commitment to capturing Turner's essence set new standards for biographical performances.

Director Brian Gibson masterfully balances the musical sequences with intense domestic scenes, creating a rhythm that mirrors Tina's own journey from victim to survivor. The film's influence can be seen in later works like Straight Outta Compton (2015) and Bohemian Rhapsody (2018), though few match its raw intensity. The decision to end with Turner's triumph rather than tragedy became a blueprint for survivor stories. SUBHEAD: Impact on Musical Biopics and Female-Led Narratives

sections.content: The film revolutionized how Hollywood approached female musicians' stories. While earlier biopics often romanticized their subjects' struggles, What's Love Got to Do with It showed the brutal reality behind the glamour. This influence can be seen in later works like I, Tonya (2017) and Judy (2019), which similarly refuse to flinch from their protagonists' hardships. The film's success also helped prove that audiences would embrace complex, difficult stories about women in the entertainment industry.
